name: Joiner-Mover-Leaver Awareness

quiz.text: What does JML stand for in the context of identity and access management?

answers.text: Just My Luck
Joiner-Mover-Leaver
Job Management Lifecycle
Join-Modify-Leave

quiz.text: What is an 'orphaned account'?

answers.text: An account that has never been used
An active account belonging to someone who has left the organization
An account with a weak password
An account shared between multiple users

quiz.text: A colleague who is leaving next week asks to borrow your login to 'finish a few things' after their access is revoked. What should you do?

answers.text: Share your password since they're a trusted colleague
Decline and suggest they request a proper access extension through their manager
Create a new shared account for the handover period
Let them use your login but change your password afterward

quiz.text: What is 'access accumulation' and why is it a security risk?

answers.text: When employees request too many password resets, creating account lockouts
When employees keep permissions from previous roles, creating excessive access that increases blast radius if compromised
When multiple employees share a single account
When employees save too many files to shared drives

quiz.text: You notice that a former employee's account is still showing activity in audit logs weeks after they left. What should you do?

answers.text: Assume IT is handling it and ignore it
Contact the former employee directly to ask about it
Report it immediately to the Security team as a potential orphaned account
Wait to see if the activity continues before taking action

quiz.text: Which of the following are your responsibilities during a role transition (as a 'Mover')? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Notify your manager of access you no longer need
Keep old access 'just in case' you need it later
Complete access certification reviews promptly
Report if you still have access to old systems after transitioning
Request temporary access through proper channels if you need old system access

steps.name: A List Somebody Sold Him
steps.description:
Bob buys credential dumps. This one came out of a hobby forum breach last November and has nothing to do with Crestfield.

He has filtered it down to the handful of people who signed up there with a work address.
steps.instructions: Open the file.

steps.name: One Name That Should Be Dead
steps.note: A password from an unrelated breach only matters if it was reused. An account belonging to a leaver only matters if it is still enabled. Neither failure is dramatic on its own.

highlighterTexts: Marcus Deane left Crestfield on 14 March. This password leaked from a forum, not from Crestfield.
Bob is betting on two ordinary failures at once: that Marcus reused the password, and that nobody switched his account off when he left.

steps.description:
Five Crestfield addresses, five passwords, all in plain text because the forum stored them that way.

One of the five belongs to somebody who left the company in March.
steps.instructions: Read the flagged line, then click Next.

steps.name: Try the Door
steps.description: Bob opens the underwriting workspace. He is not attacking it. He is going to sign in.
steps.instructions: Open the underwriting sign-in page.

steps.name: It Opens
steps.note: Five months after his last day, Marcus's account still authenticates, still carries his underwriting permissions, and still shows as Active in the directory.
steps.description:
The password Marcus used on a hobby forum is the password he used at Crestfield. The account it belongs to was never disabled.

No alert fires, because nothing unusual has happened: a valid user signed in with a valid password.
steps.instructions: Sign in with the credentials from the list.

steps.name: Take the Book
steps.description: Marcus worked in Underwriting, so his account still reaches the commercial book: policyholders, premiums, sums insured, claims history.
steps.instructions: Export the book.

steps.name: Four Thousand Policies

highlighterTexts: 4,206 commercial policies with premiums, sums insured and claims history. A competitor could price against every one of them.
Nothing here was bypassed. The account was entitled to do this, because it was never told it had stopped being an employee.

steps.description:
The export runs under Marcus's name. In every log Crestfield keeps, this is Marcus doing his job.

Bob leaves the tab open and does not come back for a while.
steps.instructions: Read the result, then click Next.

steps.name: Where Did This Go Wrong

answers.text: When Marcus reused his work password on a hobby forum
answers.explanation: Password reuse made the credential available, but a disabled account would have made the credential worthless. It is a contributing failure, not the deciding one.

answers.text: When Marcus's account was left enabled after his last day
answers.explanation: Deprovisioning is what converts a former employee into a former user. Without it, every credential they ever had stays live indefinitely.

answers.text: When the forum was breached
answers.explanation: Crestfield cannot control a third party's breach. It can control whether a leaver's account still works five months later.

answers.text: When the export ran without triggering an alert
answers.explanation: Monitoring would have shortened the incident, not prevented it. The account was entitled to run that export.

data.question: Marcus left in March and did nothing wrong after he left. At which point did this become possible?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: A Question From Security

email.message:
Alice,

The commercial book was exported at 02:14 last Tuesday by marcus.deane@crestfield.com.

Marcus left Crestfield on 14 March. His laptop came back, his badge was collected, and HR closed his record the same week. His IAM account was never disabled.

The sign-in came from an address we do not recognise, using a password that also appears in a public breach list. We are treating the account as compromised.

You own access reviews for Enterprise Risk. Please open the account directory, disable the account, and tell us what you find: https://iam.crestfield.com/login

Security Operations
email.subject: Underwriting book exported by a leaver account

steps.description: The underwriting book has turned up in a competitor's renewal quotes. Security traced the export and wants to understand the account that ran it.
steps.instructions: Open the email and read it.

steps.name: Three Things Happened, One Did Not
steps.note: A leaver checklist that tracks equipment will always look complete before the access half is done. The access half is the part with no object to hand back.

highlighterTexts: Laptop returned, badge collected, HR record closed. Offboarding felt finished because the things you can hold were all accounted for.
His IAM account was never disabled. Nobody notices an account that is still switched on, because a working account looks exactly like a correct one.

steps.description:
Everything visible was done. The laptop, the badge and the HR record were all handled the same week.

The only step with no physical object attached to it is the one that was missed.
steps.instructions: Read the highlighted section, then click Next.

steps.name: Open the Directory
steps.description: Alice opens the IAM portal from the link in the security email.
steps.instructions: Click the portal link in the email.

steps.name: Sign In
steps.description: Alice signs in to the IAM portal with her own account.
steps.instructions: Sign in to the IAM portal.

steps.name: Still On the Books

highlighterTexts: Left 14 March, account Active, last sign-in last Tuesday at 02:14. Those three facts have been sitting in one row for five months.
Compare the last row: Tomas Bergh left in February and his account reads Disabled, with his last sign-in on his last working day. That is what a completed leaver looks like.

steps.description:
The directory lists Marcus alongside current colleagues. Nothing about the row says he stopped working here five months ago except the employment column, which nobody reads.

Alice has the row in front of her and the Disable button beside it.
steps.instructions: Read the flagged row, then click Next.

steps.name: Active Versus Disabled

answers.text: Nothing, because both people have already left the company
answers.explanation: Leaving is an HR fact. The account is what decides whether a password still opens anything, and only one of these two accounts was switched off.

answers.text: Tomas's password authenticates nothing; Marcus's authenticates everything his role reached
answers.explanation: Disabling removes the identity, so the credential has nothing to sign in to. Leaving the account active preserves the whole permission set indefinitely.

answers.text: Marcus's account would be caught by monitoring because he is a leaver
answers.explanation: The account is not flagged as a leaver anywhere the sign-in path looks. To the application it is an ordinary employee account, which is why the export raised nothing.

answers.text: Both are equally risky, so disabling is mostly paperwork
answers.explanation: This is the assumption that left the account open for five months. Disabling is the single control that made the stolen password worthless.

data.question: Tomas Bergh also left Crestfield, and his account reads Disabled. Marcus Deane's reads Active. What does that difference actually change for an attacker holding either password?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Switch It Off
steps.description: In Crestfield's portal, disabling the account also revokes every session it currently holds and stops the credential from authenticating again, whoever is using it.
steps.instructions: Disable the account.

steps.name: He Goes Back For More
steps.note: Crestfield's portal disables the account and revokes its live sessions in one action, so the next thing an attacker who is already signed in clicks fails. In some identity systems disabling alone leaves issued tokens valid until they expire, so revoke sessions as part of the same step.
steps.description:
Bob's session from last week is still open in his browser. Nothing on his side has changed and he has no idea anything has happened.

He goes back for the rest of the book.
steps.instructions: Export the book again.

steps.name: Nothing There

highlighterTexts: The credential is still correct and still public. It no longer opens anything, because the account behind it is gone.
Disabling the account did what a password reset would only half do: it removed the identity, not just the secret.

steps.description: Same password. Same account. Same button.
steps.instructions: Read the result, then click Next.

steps.name: Report What You Found

variables.name: reply
variables.correctValue:
Account disabled and sessions revoked.

What I found:
- marcus.deane@crestfield.com was still enabled 5 months after his leaving date of 14 March.
- It kept his Underwriting permissions, so it could export the full commercial book.
- It sat in the directory alongside current colleagues with no visible difference except the employment column.

Why it stayed open:
- Offboarding tracked the laptop, the badge and the HR record. All three were completed that week.
- Disabling the IAM account was not tied to any of them, so nothing was left outstanding to chase.

What I am asking for:
- Make account disablement part of the same leaver ticket as equipment return, and do not let the ticket close until it is done.
- Run a monthly report of enabled accounts with no sign-in from a current employee, so an account like this surfaces in weeks rather than months.

Tomas Bergh's February leaver record was handled correctly and is a good template.

steps.description: Security asked what Alice found. The account is closed, but the reason it stayed open is the part that will repeat.
steps.instructions: Reply to Security Operations with your findings.

steps.name: What To Take Away
steps.note:
Carry this into your own transitions:
  • Leaving is not finished when the equipment comes back. Access is the half with nothing to hand over.
  • When you change roles, say what you no longer need. Nobody else can see which of your permissions went quiet.
  • An account nobody uses is not harmless. It is a working credential with no one watching it.
  • If you spot a former colleague still listed as active, report it. It reads as an admin detail and behaves like an open door.
  • Never lend your login to someone who is leaving. Their last day ends their access, not yours.
steps.description:
Marcus did not attack Crestfield. He left, handed back his laptop, and got on with his life.

The company kept his account alive for five months, and somebody who had never worked there used it to take the underwriting book.
steps.instructions: Click Next to finish.

description: When someone leaves, their access is supposed to leave with them. This exercise follows one account that nobody switched off: what a stranger does with it months later, and how the gap is found and closed.

actorDescriptions.bob: A threat actor who does not break into anything. He buys credential dumps from unrelated breaches and tries them against company systems, betting that somebody reused a password and that somebody else forgot to switch an account off.
actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a Senior Risk Analyst in the Enterprise Risk team at Crestfield Insurance. You spent two years in Underwriting before this, so you know exactly what is in the book the company keeps there.

name: Password Manager Habits

quiz.text: What is the primary benefit of using a password manager?

answers.text: It makes your computer run faster.
It allows you to use unique, complex passwords for every account without having to memorize them.
It automatically logs you into all websites without any action required.
It prevents all types of cyber attacks.

quiz.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of a strong password? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: At least 16 characters long.
Contains only lowercase letters for easy typing.
Is long and random, ideally generated by a password manager.
Based on personal information like your birthday or pet's name.
Is unique and not reused across multiple accounts.

quiz.text: How does a password manager help protect against phishing attacks?

answers.text: It blocks all emails from unknown senders.
It only autofills credentials on the exact domain where they were saved, not on lookalike fake sites.
It encrypts all your internet traffic.
It scans websites for malware before you visit them.

quiz.text: Why is password reuse considered a security risk?

answers.text: It makes passwords harder to remember.
Websites can detect reused passwords and lock your account.
If one account is compromised, attackers can use the same credentials to access all your other accounts.
Reused passwords expire faster than unique ones.

quiz.text: What should you do with your master password for a password manager? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Make it long and memorable, such as a passphrase.
Write it on a sticky note attached to your monitor for easy access.
Never reuse it for any other account or service.
Share it with your IT department so they can help if you forget it.
Store a backup copy in a secure location (like a safe) in case you forget it.

quiz.text: Before using autofill on a login page, what should you verify?

answers.text: That the website has a colorful design.
That the URL is correct and the connection is secure (HTTPS).
That you have typed your password at least once before.
That your computer's sound is turned on.

steps.name: A Forgotten Password
steps.description:
It's Alice's first day back after a long vacation.

As she tries to log into the company portal, she realizes she can't remember her password. She's tried several combinations, but none of them work.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Common Mistake
steps.note: Reusing passwords or using predictable variations is one of the most common security mistakes. A breach on one site can lead to "credential stuffing" attacks on all your accounts.
steps.description:
Alice thinks back to her password habits. Like many people, she's been using variations of the same password across multiple accounts - adding numbers or special characters to a base password she can remember.

She realizes this is risky because if one account gets compromised, attackers could easily guess her other passwords.
steps.instructions: Click Next to learn about a better solution.

steps.name: Introducing the Password Manager
steps.note: Password managers eliminate the need to memorize dozens of passwords. They also prevent phishing attacks since they won't autofill credentials on fake websites.
steps.description:
Alice remembers that CypherPeak Technologies provides a password manager called KeyVault to all employees.

A password manager is a secure application that stores all your passwords in an encrypted vault. You only need to remember one master password to access all your credentials.
steps.instructions: Open the KeyVault password manager from the taskbar.

steps.name: Unlocking the Vault
steps.note: Your master password should be strong and unique - it's the key to all your other passwords. Never share it or write it down where others can find it.
steps.description:
The password manager is locked by default - this is a security feature that protects your credentials even if someone gains access to your computer.

Alice needs to enter her master password to unlock the vault. This is the one password she needs to remember.
steps.instructions: Enter the master password to unlock the vault.

steps.name: Exploring the Vault
steps.description:
Alice opens KeyVault and sees several saved entries from when IT set up her account. Each entry contains a website, username, and securely stored password.

The passwords are hidden by default - you need to click to reveal them. This prevents shoulder surfing in shared office spaces.
steps.instructions: Click on the "Company Portal" entry to view its details.

steps.name: Revealing the Password
steps.description:
Alice wants to check her saved password for the Company Portal. The passwords are hidden by default to prevent shoulder surfing.

To view the actual password, she needs to click the reveal button (eye icon).
steps.instructions: Click the eye icon to reveal the password.

steps.name: Understanding Password Strength
steps.note: A strong password should be at least 16 characters long and random, not built from words or patterns you could guess. Password managers make this easy by generating and remembering such passwords for you.
steps.description:
Alice sees that her password is "OldPassword123" - a weak password that was set when her account was first created. Weak passwords like this are vulnerable to:
  • Dictionary attacks (using common words)
  • Brute force attacks (trying all combinations)
  • Social engineering (guessing based on personal info)
She decides to replace it: first she signs in to the portal and opens its password-change page, then she generates the new password in KeyVault.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Logging into the Portal
steps.description:
Alice opens the browser and goes to the company portal's login page. The password manager can fill in her stored credentials there.

Autofill saves time and prevents typos.
steps.instructions: Open the browser and navigate to the company portal login page.

steps.name: Using Autofill Safely
steps.note: Password managers provide an extra layer of phishing protection - they only autofill on the exact domain where the credentials were saved. Fake lookalike sites won't trigger autofill.
steps.description:
Alice is on the login page. When she clicks on the email field, the password manager detects the saved credentials and shows an autofill suggestion. Before autofilling, always verify:
  • The URL is correct (no typosquatting)
  • The connection is secure (HTTPS)
  • The page looks legitimate
steps.instructions: Click on the email field to see the autofill popup, then select "Company Portal" to fill in the credentials.

steps.name: Opening Account Settings
steps.description:
Alice has successfully logged in. Now she opens the account settings page, where the portal lets her change her password.

Before she types anything there, she'll generate the new password in KeyVault.
steps.instructions: Navigate to the account settings page to change your password.

steps.name: Generating a Strong Password
steps.description:
The password-change form is open. Alice switches back to KeyVault, which includes a built-in password generator that creates random, cryptographically secure passwords.

These generated passwords are impossible to guess and unique to each account. Since the password manager remembers them, you don't need to memorize them yourself.
steps.instructions: In KeyVault, edit the Company Portal entry, then open the generator to create a strong new password.

steps.name: Password Generated
steps.note: Length is what does the work, so take the longest password the site will accept. 16 characters is a floor, not a ceiling, and NIST asks services to allow at least 64. A random generator gives you unpredictability without any need to satisfy a character-type checklist. The password manager remembers it, so length costs you nothing.
steps.description:
Excellent! The password generator created a strong, random password. Notice how it includes:
  • At least 16 characters, drawn at random
  • A mix of uppercase and lowercase letters
  • Numbers and special characters
The mix is a by-product of random generation, not a rule you have to satisfy. NIST advises services against forcing character-type requirements, because they push people toward predictable patterns like Password1!. What actually defeats brute force here is length plus randomness: this password would take billions of years to crack. Alice saves it to the vault now, before she changes it on the site, so the new password never exists only in a web form.
steps.instructions: Click "Update Password" to replace the weak password on your Company Portal entry.

steps.name: Setting the New Password
steps.description:
Alice returns to the account settings page in the browser. She'll use the strong password she just generated to replace her weak one.

Her vault entry already holds the new password, so once she submits, the site and the vault will match.
steps.instructions: Enter your current password, then the new password in both fields, and click Update Password.

steps.name: Password Manager Best Practices
steps.note: The master password is the single point of failure for your password manager. Make it long and memorable (a passphrase works well), and never reuse it anywhere else.
steps.description:
Alice has successfully updated her password. Here are key best practices for using a password manager:
  • Use a unique, strong password for each account
  • Enable two-factor authentication where available
  • Never share your master password
  • Keep your password manager software updated
  • Regularly audit the vault and replace weak, reused or exposed passwords
steps.instructions: Click Next to complete the training.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.description:
Alice now has a much stronger security posture. By using a password manager, she can:
  • Generate unique, complex passwords for every account
  • Never worry about forgetting passwords again
  • Protect against phishing with domain-aware autofill
  • Quickly update compromised credentials
Remember: A password manager is one of the most effective tools for personal cybersecurity.
steps.instructions: Click the Next button to proceed to the quiz.

description: Learn how to use a password manager to securely store and manage your credentials. This exercise covers creating strong passwords, organizing entries, and safely using autofill features to protect your accounts from unauthorized access.

name: Credential Stuffing Awareness

quiz.text: What is credential stuffing?

answers.text: A phishing attack that tricks users into revealing passwords
An automated attack using stolen credentials from one breach to access other accounts
A brute-force attack that guesses random passwords
A malware that steals passwords from your computer

quiz.text: Why does password reuse make credential stuffing so effective?

answers.text: People use simple passwords that are easy to guess
Attackers can access multiple accounts with a single leaked password
Password managers store all passwords in one place
Websites don't encrypt passwords properly

quiz.text: What should you do when you receive a data breach notification? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Change the password for the breached service
Change passwords on any other accounts that used the same password
Enable MFA on the breached account and other important accounts
Ignore it if you don't use that service anymore
Wait to see if anything suspicious happens before taking action

quiz.text: Which combination of defenses best protects against credential stuffing?

answers.text: A longer password and security questions
Unique passwords for each account plus multi-factor authentication
Changing your password every 30 days
Using a VPN when logging into accounts

quiz.text: How do attackers typically obtain the credentials used in credential stuffing attacks?

answers.text: By watching users type their passwords
From data breaches at other companies and services
By guessing based on personal information
By hacking into password managers

quiz.text: What is the main advantage of using a password manager to prevent credential stuffing?

answers.text: It encrypts your passwords so they can't be stolen
It generates and stores unique passwords for every account
It automatically changes your passwords every week
It blocks suspicious login attempts

steps.name: Welcome to TechNova Solutions

email.message:
Dear Valued Customer,

We are writing to inform you of a security incident that may have affected your StreamFlix account.

What happened: On December 15, 2024, we discovered unauthorized access to one of our databases containing user information.

Information potentially exposed:
  • Email addresses
  • Encrypted passwords (may be decrypted over time)
  • Account creation dates
What we're doing: We have reset all passwords and are requiring users to create new ones upon login.

What you should do:
  • Change your StreamFlix password (required)
  • If you use this password anywhere else, change it there too
  • Enable two-factor authentication
We sincerely apologize for any concern this may cause.

StreamFlix Security Team
email.subject: Important: StreamFlix Security Incident Notice

steps.description: You take security seriously - you always lock your computer and never click suspicious links. But like many people, you have a favorite password that you use across several accounts. It's complex enough to be secure, so why not reuse it?
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: A Normal Tuesday Morning

email.message:
Dear Alice,

We detected a successful login to your TechNova account from an unfamiliar location, right after two failed attempts:
  • Time: Today, 3:47 AM EST
  • Location: Bucharest, Romania
  • IP Address: 185.234.72.xxx
  • Attempts: 2 failed attempts followed by 1 successful login
Action Required: If this was not you, please contact IT Security immediately at security@technova.io or call ext. 4400.

A temporary hold has been placed on your account pending verification.

IT Security Team
email.subject: Alert: Unusual Login Activity Detected

steps.description:
It's Tuesday morning. You're working on a feature release when an email notification appears - something about suspicious activity on your account.

You don't recall doing anything unusual. Must be a routine security alert.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox and read the security alert.

steps.name: The Alarming Details
steps.note: Credential stuffing attacks don't require phishing. Attackers use stolen credentials from other breaches and automated tools to test them across thousands of sites.

highlighterTexts: 2 failed attempts followed by 1 successful login - a bot tried a couple of leaked passwords for your address, and one of them worked.
The login came from Bucharest, Romania at 3:47 AM - clearly not you.
This wasn't random guessing. Someone had your exact password from another source.

steps.description:
Your heart sinks. Bucharest? You've never been there. And only two failed attempts before a successful login at 3:47 AM?

Someone definitely accessed your account. But how? You haven't clicked any suspicious links. You haven't shared your password with anyone.

Then you remember - last month, you got an email about a data breach at StreamFlix, that video streaming service you signed up for years ago. You use the same password there as you do for your TechNova account...
steps.instructions: Review the alarming details in the security alert.

steps.name: Connecting the Dots
steps.description:
You scroll through your old emails and find the StreamFlix breach notification from last month. It mentioned that email addresses and passwords were exposed.

At the time, you changed your StreamFlix password but didn't think to update your other accounts that used the same password. Now you realize - attackers took those leaked credentials and tested them against other services, including TechNova.
steps.instructions: Read the StreamFlix data breach notification email.

steps.name: The Red Flag You Missed

highlighterTexts: The email explicitly warned: 'If you use this password anywhere else, change it there too'
Password reuse means a single breach can compromise ALL accounts using that password.
Attackers know most people reuse passwords - it's the foundation of credential stuffing attacks.

steps.description: Looking at the StreamFlix email again, you notice a critical warning you glossed over at the time.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted warning in the breach notification.

steps.name: Contacting IT Security
steps.description: Alice needs to report this immediately. She picks up her phone to call IT Security using the extension from the original alert - not any number from external emails.
steps.instructions: Open your phone contacts and call IT Security.

steps.name: Follow-Up from IT Security

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting the suspicious activity on your account. Our initial investigation confirms unauthorized access from Romania using valid credentials.

Immediate Actions Required:
  1. File an Incident Report - Log in to the Security Portal and document what happened
  2. Complete Security Training - A mandatory credential stuffing awareness module has been assigned to you
Your temporary credentials:
  • Email: alice@technova.io
  • Password: TempSecure2024!
Please complete both tasks within the next 24 hours.

IT Security Team
Ext. 4400
email.subject: Action Required: Incident Report & Security Training

steps.description: After the call, IT Security sends a follow-up email with next steps and temporary credentials to Alice's personal address, which she has open on her desktop.
steps.instructions: Read the follow-up email from IT Security.

steps.name: The Investigation Begins

highlighterTexts: IT Security confirmed unauthorized access from Romania using your valid credentials.
You need to file an incident report and complete mandatory security training.
Temporary credentials have been provided - use these to access the Security Portal.

steps.description:
IT Security confirms that your account was accessed from Romania using valid credentials. The attacker accessed your email, downloaded several documents, and attempted to access the company VPN before the security systems flagged the unusual behavior.

Fortunately, the security team detected the intrusion quickly. But the damage assessment is still underway.
steps.instructions: Review the key details in the IT Security follow-up email.

steps.name: Understanding the Attack
steps.note: Credential stuffing attacks are largely automated. One leaked password that you reuse could be tested against hundreds of sites within hours of a breach.
steps.description: The security analyst explains how credential stuffing works: 1. Data Breach: Attackers obtain leaked credentials from a breach (like StreamFlix) 2. Credential Lists: They compile massive lists of email/password combinations 3. Automated Testing: Bots test these credentials against thousands of other sites 4. Account Takeover: When credentials work, they access and exploit those accounts This isn't targeted hacking - it's automated mass testing of stolen credentials.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Filing the Incident Report
steps.description: IT Security asks Alice to file a formal incident report to document the compromise and help protect others.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Security Portal using the temporary credentials from the email.

steps.name: Documenting the Incident

variables.name: issue
variables.correctValue:
My TechNova account was compromised via credential stuffing. Attackers used my password from the StreamFlix data breach (December 15, 2024) to access my account at 3:47 AM from Romania (IP: 185.234.72.xxx). I used the same password on both accounts.

The attacker accessed my email and downloaded documents before security detected the intrusion. I had ignored the StreamFlix breach warning to change passwords on other accounts.

steps.description: Alice documents the credential stuffing attack, including the source breach and the timeline of events.
steps.instructions: Complete the incident report with details of the credential stuffing attack.

steps.name: Mandatory Security Training
steps.description: As part of the incident response, IT Security requires Alice to complete a brief training module on credential stuffing prevention.
steps.instructions: Click the training link to begin.

steps.name: The Scale of the Problem

highlighterTexts: These four facts show why password reuse is so dangerous.
Password reuse is common, and it is exactly what credential stuffing exploits: one leaked password opens every account that shares it.
Stolen credentials circulate in huge collections, so assume any password you have reused has already been exposed.

steps.description: The training explains why credential stuffing works: Reused passwords mean one leak opens every account that shares it Leaked credentials from past breaches circulate in huge collections on the dark web Automated tools try each stolen pair against thousands of sites Rare hits still add up: only a small share of attempts succeed, but across millions of stolen credentials that means thousands of compromised accounts.

steps.name: What To Take Away

  • A reset password ends an incident. Removed access prevents the next one.
